title: Gas pressure from particle collisions
keyIdea: Gas particles move fast in all directions and keep hitting the walls of their container. Each hit is a tiny push, and gas pressure is the total force of those hits on each square metre of wall. Pressure rises when there are more particles, when the gas is hotter (faster particles hit harder and more often) or when the same gas is squashed into less space.

kid: A gas is made of tiny particles. They zoom about in every direction. They keep crashing into the walls of their box. Each crash gives the wall a tiny push.
Billions of crashes happen every second. Together they push hard on every wall: top, bottom and sides. This push on each bit of wall is called gas pressure.

You can make the pressure go up in three ways. Add more particles, so there are more crashes. Heat the gas, so the particles go faster and hit harder and more often. Or squash the gas into less space, so the particles reach the walls more often.
Heating does not make the particles bigger. They stay the same size. They just move faster. Cooling slows them down, so the pressure drops.
adult: In England this joins two Key Stage 3 physics topics: the particle model and pressure in fluids. It leads into the GCSE link between molecular motion, temperature and gas pressure. Pressure is force divided by area. It is measured in pascals (Pa). Air at sea level is about 100 kPa.

Gas particles move randomly at high speed. When one hits a wall, it changes direction. That change in momentum puts a force on the wall. Pressure is the total force of all the hits on each square metre. Because the motion is random, a gas pushes equally on every wall, not only downwards.

Three changes raise the pressure. Adding particles gives more hits each second. Heating raises the mean kinetic energy, so particles hit harder and more often. Squashing the gas means walls are hit more often. At a fixed temperature, halving the volume doubles the pressure.

A common misconception is that heated particles expand and press on the walls. They stay the same size; only their speed changes. Another slip is to say pressure comes from particles hitting each other. Those collisions happen, but wall hits make the pressure.

familyTip: Next time you pump up a bike or football, ask: why does it get harder to push? Then feel a ball on a frosty morning and talk about why it is a bit softer than on a hot day.

visual.caption: Does it raise or lower the gas pressure? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the walls gas pushes on, then pump, heat and squash the gas while a pressure gauge responds.

practice.prompt: What causes the pressure of a gas on its container?
practice.hint: Think about what the moving particles do when they reach a wall.
practice.explain: Each particle that hits a wall gives it a tiny push. All the hits together make the pressure.

practice.prompt: A box of gas is at {p} kPa. You pump in more gas until there are twice as many particles. The box and temperature stay the same. What is the new pressure in kPa?
practice.hint: Twice the particles means twice as many hits each second.
practice.explain: Double the particles, double the hits: {p} × 2 = {=2*p} kPa.

practice.prompt: A sealed can of gas is heated. Why does the pressure rise?
choices: The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
The particles grow and push on the can
practice.hint: Heating gives particles more kinetic energy.
practice.explain: Faster particles hit harder and more often. They do not change size, and the can is sealed so no particles are added.

practice.prompt: A syringe holds gas at {p} kPa. The end is blocked and the plunger squashes the gas into half the space. The temperature stays the same. What is the new pressure in kPa?
practice.hint: In half the space, particles reach the walls twice as often.
practice.explain: Half the volume, double the pressure: {p} × 2 = {=2*p} kPa.

pool.prompt: Which walls of a box of gas feel the pressure?
pool.hint: Gas particles move in every direction.
pool.explain: Particles move in all directions, so they hit and push on every wall equally.

pool.prompt: A balloon is put in a freezer and gets smaller. What happened to the particles?
choices: They slowed down, so they hit the inside less hard and less often
pool.explain: Colder particles move more slowly, so they push less on the rubber and the balloon shrinks. They do not shrink or stop.

pool.prompt: What is the unit of pressure?
pool.hint: It is named after Blaise Pascal.
pool.explain: Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals: 1 Pa is 1 newton on each square metre.

pool.prompt: Why does a deodorant can say do not heat?
choices: Heating raises the pressure inside and it could burst
pool.hint: What happens to particle speed when gas is heated?
pool.explain: Hotter particles hit the inside of the can harder and more often. The pressure could get high enough to burst it.

pool.prompt: Gas pressure is caused by particles hitting each other. Is this right?
choices: No, it is caused by particles hitting the walls
pool.hint: Pressure is a push on a surface.
pool.explain: Particles do collide with each other, but the pressure on a container comes from their hits on its walls.

pool.prompt: Why is a bike tyre harder after you pump it up?
choices: More air particles inside make more hits on the tyre each second
pool.hint: What does each push of the pump add?
pool.explain: Each pump adds particles. More particles in the same space means more hits, so higher pressure.

pool.prompt: Gas in a sealed box is at {p} kPa. It is squashed into a third of the space at the same temperature. What is the new pressure in kPa?
pool.hint: A third of the space means hits happen 3 times as often.
pool.explain: A third of the volume gives 3 times the pressure: {p} × 3 = {=3*p} kPa.

pool.prompt: A tyre is at {p} kPa. Half of the air is let out, at the same temperature. What is the new pressure in kPa?
pool.hint: Half the particles make half as many hits.
pool.explain: Half the particles in the same space: {p} ÷ 2 = {=p/2} kPa.

pool.prompt: A gas is given twice the space at the same temperature. What happens to the pressure?
pool.hint: With more room, particles reach the walls less often.
pool.explain: Twice the volume means half as many hits on each square metre each second, so the pressure halves.
